sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: The aim of this study is to assess positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)–guided neoadjuvant treatment with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy/chemoradiotherapy in patients with resectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC).

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: RATIONALE-213, a multicenter, open-label, two-cohort phase II study, enrolled 70 patients with resectable ESCC. After one induction chemotherapy cycle, patients were categorized as PET responders (PET maximum standardized uptake value decrease ≥35%) or PET nonresponders (<35%). Subsequently, all patients received three cycles of tislelizumab 200 mg intravenously. In addition, PET responders received chemotherapy and PET nonresponders received chemoradiotherapy as neoadjuvant treatment followed by surgery. The primary endpoint was the pathologic complete response (pCR) rate.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: As of October 25, 2024 (median follow-up 25.5 months), pCR rates were 30% [95% confidence interval (CI), 11.9–54.3] in PET responders and 34.4% (95% CI, 18.6–53.2) in PET nonresponders. Higher pCR rates were associated with higher baseline programmed cell death ligand 1 tumor area positivity scores in both cohorts. One-year disease-free survival rates were 79% and 74.2%, and event-free survival rates were 87.1% and 67.8%, respectively. Any-grade and grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAE) occurred in 93.3% and 50% of PET responders and 97.5% and 82.5% of PET nonresponders, with no new safety signals. The most common grade ≥3 TRAE was decreased neutrophil count (36.7% and 70%, respectively).

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Tislelizumab with chemotherapy/chemoradiotherapy as neoadjuvant treatment for resectable ESCC yielded promising pCR rates and favorable survival outcomes with a tolerable safety profile in both PET/CT-guided responders and PET nonresponders.

boxed-text.p: The phase II study RATIONALE-213 reports the efficacy and safety of positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)–guided neoadjuvant treatment with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy in patients with resectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). This PET/CT-guided approach allows for tailored treatment based on response to induction chemotherapy, potentially optimizing clinical outcomes while minimizing toxicity. The promising pathologic complete response (pCR) rates and favorable survival outcomes observed in both PET/CT-assessed responders and nonresponders suggest that this strategy may help optimize neoadjuvant selection. Furthermore, higher pCR rates were observed in patients with higher baseline programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) tumor area positivity scores in both cohorts, suggesting PD-L1 expression may be a potential predictive biomarker for response to neoadjuvant tislelizumab-based therapy in patients with ESCC. These findings contribute to the growing evidence for neoadjuvant immunotherapy in ESCC. The tolerable safety profile of this regimen supports its potential integration into clinical practice, which may lead to improved outcomes for patients with ESCC.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Esophageal cancer ranks among the most prevalent cancer types and is the sixth leading cause of cancer-related deaths globally (1). Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is the most common histologic subtype worldwide (1, 2).

For early-stage ESCC, endoscopic resection is the initial recommended treatment, with surgery indicated for histologic margin infiltration or high-risk features, including lymph node metastasis (3). For locally advanced resectable ESCC, preoperative chemoradiation followed by surgery is the standard of care (3) in the United States and Europe. Previous studies, like CROSS (4, 5) and NEOCRTEC5010 (6), have demonstrated improvement in overall survival (OS) with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) followed by surgery versus surgery alone in ESCC. However, regional variations exist in treatment approaches, with China and Japan also recognizing neoadjuvant chemotherapy as a standard-of-care option (7, 8).

Although neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery offers survival benefits over surgery alone (9), comparative survival benefits between neoadjuvant chemotherapy and nCRT remain unclear. Although postoperative complication frequency is similar between both approaches, patients receiving nCRT experienced more severe complications and higher postoperative mortality (10–12). Consequently, safety concerns often favor preoperative chemotherapy alone over nCRT in clinical practice.

Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) studies have demonstrated that changes in the maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) following induction chemotherapy have good predictive value for treatment response in esophageal cancer (13–15). PET responders (defined as patients with an SUVmax decrease ≥35%) achieve higher pathologic complete response (pCR) rates and significantly better survival outcomes than PET nonresponders (defined as patients with an SUVmax decrease <35%). This indicates that PET responders have a more favorable prognosis and are not at as high a risk compared with PET nonresponders. This prognostic difference supports tailoring treatment intensity based on PET response, potentially sparing responders from radiotherapy toxicities without compromising outcomes, whereas nonresponders may require more intensive approaches to improve survival (13–17).

Tislelizumab, an mAb targeting the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), has demonstrated survival improvement in patients with advanced or metastatic ESCC. Tislelizumab is approved in combination with chemotherapy for first-line treatment of unresectable ESCC based on the results of the RATIONALE-306 study (18) and as monotherapy in the second line for unresectable or metastatic ESCC after prior chemotherapy that did not include a PD-1/programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor based on the results of the RATIONALE-302 study (19).

RATIONALE-213 (NCT04974047) was a prospective, multicenter, open-label, two-cohort phase II study conducted in China evaluating the efficacy and safety of PET/CT-guided neoadjuvant treatment with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy/CRT in patients with resectable ESCC (20). Here, we report the study’s final analysis (data cutoff: October 25, 2024) with pCR as the primary endpoint.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: In RATIONALE-213, eligible patients were consecutively enrolled at eight centers in China from August 19, 2021, to October 20, 2022. After baseline 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT evaluation followed by one cycle of induction doublet chemotherapy (cisplatin and paclitaxel), patients who underwent a second PET/CT scan (days 15–21) were grouped into two cohorts based on the change in PET SUVmax in the primary tumor. PET responders (≥35% decrease in PET SUVmax) received tislelizumab (200 mg i.v.; once every 3 weeks; three cycles) plus doublet chemotherapy (cisplatin and paclitaxel, two cycles). PET nonresponders (<35% decrease in PET SUVmax) received tislelizumab (200 mg i.v. every 3 weeks, three cycles) plus investigator-chosen doublet chemotherapy (paclitaxel plus cisplatin/5-fluorouracil plus cisplatin, two cycles) plus radiotherapy (40 Gy/20 fractions; Supplementary Fig. S1).

After completion of neoadjuvant therapy, patients were reassessed for resectability before surgery. Surgical specimens were assessed for pathologic response [major pathologic response (MPR) and pCR] by a local pathologist. Safety was assessed throughout the study by monitoring and recording all adverse events according to NCI Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0. A detailed description of the study design is available in the study protocol in the Supplementary Material.

The study was conducted after obtaining approval from the relevant institutional review board or independent ethics committee for each study site (Supplementary Table S1). The study was conducted in accordance with the International Council for Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice Guideline, the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and local laws and regulations. All patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: The study included adults with histologically confirmed, resectable ESCC with stage cT1-2N+M0 and cT3NanyM0 (American Joint Committee on Cancer, Eighth Edition; ref. 21). Participants were eligible for an R0 resection with curative intent and had evaluable disease as assessed by the investigator per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST v1.1), an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) of 0 or 1, and adequate hematologic and organ function. Exclusion criteria included a history of fistula/perforation risk, autoimmune diseases, recent malignancies, systemic immunosuppressant use, and prior ESCC treatment. Enrollment occurred regardless of PD-L1 expression status. The cohort represented the target population of patients with resectable ESCC in China (Supplementary Table S2). Full eligibility criteria are described in the study protocol in the Supplementary Material.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: Tislelizumab (200 mg i.v. every 3 weeks) was administered on day 1 of cycles 2 to 4. Chemotherapy consisted of cisplatin (80 mg/m2 i.v. on day 1 or 2 of cycles 1–3) and paclitaxel (135 mg/m2 i.v. on day 1 of cycles 1–3; Supplementary Fig. S1). The chemotherapy regimen could be switched for PET nonresponders from paclitaxel plus cisplatin to 5-fluorouracil (1,000 mg/m2/cycle intravenously, days 1–4 of cycles 2 and 3) plus cisplatin based on the investigator’s decision. These patients also received radiotherapy (40 Gy/20 fractions), with priority given to maintaining continuous treatment despite potential chemotherapy interruptions due to toxicity (Supplementary Fig. S1). Alternate doses and dosing schedules for radiotherapy were allowed according to local and institutional guidelines. Surgery was performed within 4 to 6 weeks after the last neoadjuvant treatment (PET responders: last dose of chemotherapy; PET nonresponders: last dose of CRT). Necessary concomitant medications and therapies were allowed.

All available tumor samples underwent centralized, retrospective assessment for PD-L1 tumor area positivity (TAP) scores by pathologists using the VENTANA PD-L1 (SP263) Assay (Roche Diagnostics). The TAP score was defined as the total percentage of tumor area (tumor and any desmoplastic stroma) with PD-L1 staining on tumor cells and immune cells at any intensity.

sec.title: Endpoints and assessments
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the pCR rate, defined as the proportion of patients with the absence of residual tumor in the area of the resected primary tumor and all resected lymph nodes (ypT0N0) after completion of neoadjuvant therapy followed by surgery, as assessed by the investigator in the efficacy-evaluable analysis set. Secondary endpoints included the 1-year disease-free survival (DFS) rate, 1-year event-free survival (EFS) rate, objective response rate (ORR) before surgery, R0 resection rate as assessed by the investigator, and safety. Exploratory endpoints included OS, MPR rate, and biomarker analyses.

Disease follow-up tumor assessments were performed using neck, chest, and abdominal CT scans every 3 months after surgery for the first 2 years and then every 6 months beginning in the third year based on RECIST v1.1.

DFS was defined as the time from the first date of no disease to local or distant recurrence or death due to any cause, whichever occurred first. The 1-year DFS rate was defined as the proportion of patients free from disease events at the end of the first year after the first date of no disease (R0 resection as the surgical outcome). The analysis of DFS was based on the efficacy-evaluable analysis set. For DFS analysis, patients were censored at the date of the last adequate tumor assessment with no evidence of recurrence if they did not experience recurrence or death. Patients who started new anticancer therapy without documented recurrence were censored at the date of the last adequate tumor assessment before the initiation of new therapy. Patients with no postsurgical assessments were censored at the date of surgery.

EFS was defined as the time from the first dose date to any of the following events, whichever occurred first: progression of disease that precludes definitive surgery, local or distant recurrence, or death due to any cause. The 1-year EFS rate was defined as the proportion of patients free from EFS events. The analysis of EFS was based on the safety analysis set. For patients who did not undergo surgery, those with progression that precluded surgery were counted as having an EFS event at the time of documented progression. Patients who refused surgery without evidence of progression were censored at the date of the decision not to proceed with surgery. For patients with delayed surgery, the censoring was based on the planned surgery date (last dose of chemotherapy/CRT + 6 weeks).

Recurrence was classified as local when it occurred at the anastomosis site or regional lymph nodes and as distant when it involved extraregional lymph node metastasis, distant organ metastasis, or pleural/peritoneal dissemination. All recurrences were confirmed by radiologic and/or histopathologic methods.

R0 resection was defined as the complete surgical removal of a tumor in which no microscopic or macroscopic disease remained at the surgical margins. R0 resection rate was defined as the proportion of patients with R0 resection and was summarized by cohort in the efficacy-evaluable analysis set.

ORR by investigator was defined as the percentage of patients with measurable disease at baseline who had a complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) before surgery as assessed by investigators per RECIST v1.1. Patients with no postbaseline response assessment (for any reason) before surgery were considered to have no tumor response.
MPR rate was defined as the proportion of patients with ≤10% residual viable tumor in the resected primary tumor and all resected lymph nodes after completion of neoadjuvant therapy.

All patients underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging at baseline and again 15 to 21 days after the start of induction chemotherapy. The study protocol required that the same 18F-FDG PET/CT scanner be used for both baseline and follow-up scans whenever possible, which was achieved in 94.3% of patients. Response was assessed locally based on the percentage change in SUVmax in the primary tumor. Patients with a decrease in SUVmax ≥35% were classified as PET responders, whereas those with <35% were classified as PET nonresponders. Response assessment was performed at each participating site according to institutional standard operating procedures. As this was a phase II study with a limited sample size, central review of 18F-FDG PET/CT and formal cross-center harmonization were not implemented. Similarly, standardized acquisition parameters, reconstruction algorithms, and SUV normalization methods were not centrally specified but followed institutional guidelines at each site. Staff in all participating centers were qualified and experienced in esophageal cancer management and 18F-FDG PET/CT assessment. All study personnel received protocol-specific training prior to study initiation. They performed these processes according to site-specific standard operating procedures or guidelines.
Pathologic assessment of surgical specimens was performed by local pathologists at each participating center following institutional standard operating procedures, without central review.

sec.title: Biomarker sample collection and analysis
sec.p: Tissue samples were collected at screening and at surgery. pCR samples at surgery were not collected.

Hematoxylin and eosin images were marked for macrodissection of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue by a pathologist prior to RNA extraction. Then, RNA purification, reverse transcription, library construction, and sequencing were performed. Captured coding regions of the transcriptome from total RNA were prepared using the TruSeq RNA Exome Library Preparation Kit (Illumina, Inc.). The library was sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 system (Illumina, Inc.; RRID: SCR_016387, https://www.illumina.com/systems/sequencing-platforms/novaseq.html) following Illumina-provided protocols for 2 × 150 paired-end sequencing. Raw sequencing reads were then trimmed for adapters and low-quality bases using Trimmomatic (version 0.39; RRID: SCR_011848, https://scicrunch.org/resources/Any/search?q=SCR_011848&l=SCR_011848; ref. 22). The processed reads were then mapped to the human genome GRCh38 using STAR (version 2.7.9; RRID: SCR_004463, https://code.google.com/archive/p/rna-star/; ref. 23) with default parameters, followed by gene expression quantification using RSEM (version 1.3.1; (RRID: SCR_013027, https://scicrunch.org/resources/Any/search?q=SCR_013027&l=SCR_013027; ref. 24), normalized to transcripts per million based on gene length and library size.

Gene signature scores were then calculated using the single-sample gene set enrichment analysis method implemented in the gene set variation analysis package (version 1.44.5; RRID: SCR_021058, https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/GSVA.html; ref. 25). A total of 52 patients (74.3%) had an evaluable gene expression profile (GEP), whereas a total of 38 patients (54.3%) had both evaluable efficacy and an evaluable GEP.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The efficacy-evaluable analysis set included all patients who received neoadjuvant treatment followed by surgery. The safety analysis set included all enrolled patients who received at least one dose of any component of the study drugs. Approximately 65 patients were planned for enrollment, with an expected distribution of 25 patients in the PET responder cohort (cohort A) and 40 patients in the PET nonresponder cohort (cohort B), allowing for approximately 10% of patients not receiving surgery.

The pCR rate assumptions were based on historical studies. For PET responders, historical pCR rates ranged from 21.9% to 31.8% (13–15), and we assumed a pCR rate of 37% for cohort A. With 23 evaluable patients, this provided a 66.2% probability of observing a pCR rate exceeding historical rates.

For PET nonresponders, historical pCR rates ranged from 4% to 13.6% (13–15), and we assumed a pCR rate of 22% for cohort B. With 35 evaluable patients, this provided a 91% probability of observing a pCR rate exceeding historical rates.

For pCR rates, 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using the Clopper–Pearson method. A sensitivity analysis of the pCR rates was also performed in the safety analysis set, and those patients who had not received surgery were treated as not having a pCR (non-pCR). Kaplan–Meier methodology was used to estimate the median and quantiles (Q1 and Q3) of DFS, EFS, OS, and the event-free rates at 12 and 36 months. The 95% CIs for the median and other quantiles of DFS, EFS, and OS were estimated using the Brookmeyer and Crowley method. The 95% CIs for event-free rates were estimated using Greenwood’s formula. The ORR was summarized with descriptive statistics by cohort, and the corresponding two-sided 95% CIs were calculated using the Clopper–Pearson exact method. A sensitivity analysis of the ORR was also performed in the safety analysis set, regardless of whether patients had measurable disease at baseline. Statistical analyses for clinical endpoints were performed using SAS version 9.4 software (RRID: SCR_008567, https://scicrunch.org/resolver/RRID:SCR_008567). Wilcoxon rank-sum exact tests were used in statistical analyses for PD-L1 immunohistochemistry and the comparison of GEP between subgroups using R version 4.4.0 software (RRID: SCR_001905, https://www.r-project.org/). Two-sided nominal P values are reported consistently throughout this article. Statistical significance was defined as P values < 0.1 for all GEP analyses due to the exploratory nature of these analyses and the limited sample size.

sec.title: Patient demographic and baseline characteristics
sec.p: At data cutoff (October 25, 2024), the median study follow-up duration was 25.5 months (range: 3.6–37.3 months). Of the 70 patients enrolled, treatment was completed in 64 (91.4%), and no patients remained in the study in both cohorts. Detailed disposition of study patients is shown in Fig. 1. The median age of all enrolled patients was 64 years (range: 47–79 years; 67.5 years for PET responders and 63.5 years for PET nonresponders), with 34 patients (48.6%) aged ≥65 years [18 (60%) PET responders and 16 (40%) PET nonresponders]. Most patients were male (88.6%; 80% of PET responders and 95% of PET nonresponders). More than half of the patients had a baseline ECOG PS of 1 (54.3%; 50% of PET responders and 57.5% of PET nonresponders). All patients were Chinese (Table 1).

sec.p: Of the 70 patients enrolled, 48 (68.6%) had stage III disease at initial diagnosis. No patients had metastatic disease at study entry. Twenty-two (31.4%) patients had a PD-L1 TAP score ≥10%, 36 (51.4%) had a PD-L1 TAP score <10%, and 12 (17.1%) had unknown PD-L1 status. The proportion of patients with unknown status was relatively high as PD-L1 expression was not an enrollment criterion.

sec.title: Treatment exposure
sec.p: All patients received induction chemotherapy; 30 were PET responders and 40 were PET nonresponders. The total number of patients treated with tislelizumab was 69 (98.6%): 30 (100%) PET responders and 39 (97.5%) PET nonresponders (Fig. 1). Among the 30 PET responders, 29 (96.7%) completed three cycles of tislelizumab (Supplementary Table S3), and 27 (90%) completed chemotherapy (paclitaxel and cisplatin; Supplementary Table S4). Among the 40 PET nonresponders, 34 (85%) completed three cycles of tislelizumab (Supplementary Table S3) and chemotherapy (paclitaxel and cisplatin; Supplementary Table S4), and 34 (85%) completed 40 Gy of radiotherapy (Supplementary Table S5). Among PET responders and PET nonresponders, 52 (74.3%) patients received surgery (baseline characteristics of surgical and nonsurgical patients by PET response status are included in Supplementary Table S6; a summary of surgeries is presented in Supplementary Table S7).

sec.title: Pathologic response by local pathologist
sec.p: Analysis of pathologic response by the local pathologist in the efficacy-evaluable analysis set showed that among the 30 PET responders, 20 (66.7%) underwent surgery, with a pCR rate of 30% (n = 6/20; 95% CI, 11.9–54.3; Table 2). MPR was observed in 9 PET responders (45%; 95% CI, 23.1–68.5). Among the 40 PET nonresponders, 32 (80%) underwent surgery, with a pCR rate of 34.4% (n = 11/32; 95% CI, 18.6–53.2). MPR was observed in 18 PET nonresponders (56.3%; 95% CI, 37.7–73.6). Subgroup analyses of pathologic response by baseline clinical characteristics are presented in Supplementary Table S8. The distribution of residual viable tumor percentages in non-pCR patients is illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S2. To account for potential overestimation, a sensitivity analysis was performed in the safety analysis set, in which patients who did not undergo surgery were counted as non-pCR. This yielded adjusted pCR rates of 20% (n = 6/30; 95% CI, 7.7–38.6) in PET responders and 27.5% (n = 11/40; 95% CI, 14.6–43.9) in PET nonresponders.

sec.p: Exploratory analysis showed differences in pCR rates based on PD-L1 expression. When a 1% cutoff was used, PET responders with a PD-L1 TAP score ≥1% had a pCR rate of 41.7% (5/12), whereas those with a PD-L1 TAP score <1% had no pCRs (0/5). In PET nonresponders, patients with a PD-L1 TAP score ≥1% had a pCR rate of 46.2% (6/13), whereas those with a PD-L1 TAP score <1% had a pCR rate of 16.7% (2/12). When a 10% cutoff was used, PET responders with a PD-L1 TAP score ≥10% had a pCR rate of 62.5% (5/8), whereas those with a PD-L1 TAP score <10% had no pCRs (0/9). Among PET nonresponders with a PD-L1 TAP score ≥10%, the pCR rate was 50% (3/6), whereas those with a PD-L1 TAP score <10% had a pCR rate of 26.3% (5/19; Supplementary Table S9).

sec.title: R0 resection
sec.p: The R0 resection rate by the local pathologist was 95% (19/20) in PET responders and 90.6% (29/32) in PET nonresponders. In PET responders, all surgeries (100%; 20/20) were with curative intent, and in PET nonresponders, the surgeries were with curative intent in 93.8% (30/32) of patients (Supplementary Table S7).

sec.title: ORR by investigator
sec.p: The tumor response by RECIST v1.1 was assessed by the investigator in patients with measurable disease at baseline before surgery. In PET responders and PET nonresponders, the ORR was 71.4% (95% CI, 47.8–88.7) and 42.4% (95% CI, 25.5–60.8), respectively (Supplementary Table S10). Among PET responders, CR was observed in 1 patient (4.8%), and PR was observed in 14 patients (66.7%). In PET nonresponders, CR was observed in 3 patients (9.1%), and PR was observed in 11 patients (33.3%). Waterfall plots showing the best percentage change from baseline in target lesion sum of diameters are presented in Supplementary Fig. S3.

sec.title: DFS by investigator
sec.p: The median DFS (investigator-assessed) in the efficacy-evaluable analysis set with R0 resection was not reached (NR) in both PET responders [n = 19; 95% CI, 10 to not estimable (NE)] and PET nonresponders (n = 29; 95% CI, 14.1–NE; Fig. 2A). The 1-year DFS rates in PET responders and PET nonresponders were 79% (95% CI, 47.9–92.7) and 74.2% (95% CI, 53.3–86.8), respectively.

sec.title: EFS by investigator
sec.p: The median EFS (investigator-assessed per RECIST v1.1) in the safety analysis set was NR in both PET responders (n = 30; 95% CI, 13.1–NE) and PET nonresponders (n = 40; 95% CI, 9.4–NE; Fig. 2B). The 1-year EFS rates in PET responders and PET nonresponders were 87.1% (95% CI, 64.3–95.8) and 67.8% (95% CI, 48.3–81.2), respectively.

Recurrence pattern analysis indicated distinct differences between cohorts (Supplementary Table S11). In both DFS and EFS analyses, PET responders experienced exclusively local recurrences (10.5% and 6.7%, respectively), whereas PET nonresponders had only distant recurrences (13.8% and 10%, respectively).

sec.title: OS
sec.p: As of October 25, 2024, median OS in both PET responders and PET nonresponders was NR. The 1-year OS rate was 83.3% (95% CI, 64.5–92.7) for PET responders and 76.9% (95% CI, 60.3–87.3) for PET nonresponders, respectively. The Kaplan–Meier plots for OS in the safety analysis set are shown in Supplementary Fig. S4.

sec.title: Safety and tolerability
sec.p: Treatment-related adverse events (TRAE) of all grades and grade ≥3 were reported in 28 (93.3%) and 15 (50%) PET responders, and 39 (97.5%) and 33 (82.5%) PET nonresponders, respectively (Table 3; Supplementary Table S12). The profile of grade ≥3 TRAEs reported in ≥10% of patients is in line with the known toxicity profile of chemotherapy or CRT, which included decreased neutrophil count (36.7%) among PET responders and decreased neutrophil count (70%), decreased white blood cell count (50%), decreased lymphocyte count (17.5%), and anemia (15%) among PET nonresponders. No TRAEs leading to death were reported.

sec.p: Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) of grade ≥3 related to tislelizumab were reported in 3 (10%) PET responders and 9 (22.5%) PET nonresponders. Radiotherapy-related TEAEs of any grade and grade ≥3 were reported in 19 (47.5%) and 6 (15%) nonresponders, respectively. Serious TEAEs related to tislelizumab were reported in 2 (6.7%) PET responders and 2 (5%) PET nonresponders.

Few patients experienced TEAEs leading to any treatment discontinuation [1 (3.3%) PET responder and 3 (7.5%) PET nonresponders], surgery delay [no PET responders and 4 (10%) PET nonresponders], or surgery cancellation [1 (3.3%) PET responder and no PET nonresponders]. All immune-mediated adverse events were grade 1 or 2 (Table 3).

Perioperative safety outcomes, including anastomotic complications and pulmonary complications, were comparable between cohorts (Supplementary Table S13). No deaths occurred within 30 days after surgery in the PET responder cohort, whereas 3 deaths (7.5%) occurred within 30 days after surgery in the PET nonresponder cohort. No PET responders died within 90 days after surgery compared with 5 deaths (12.5%) in the PET nonresponder cohort. Additional mortality data are presented in Supplementary Table S14.

sec.title: Biomarker analysis
sec.p: Baseline characteristics and response rates were comparable between efficacy- and GEP-evaluable populations (Supplementary Table S15). Biomarker sample collection included 58 baseline tissues (PET responders, n = 27; PET nonresponders, n = 31) and 31 surgery non-pCR tissues (PET responders, n = 14; PET nonresponders, n = 17). Baseline GEP showed that PET responders had higher expression of immune-activation genes [effector T cells, CD8+ T cells, Th1 cells, M1 macrophages, NK cells, and interferon (IFN) gamma], whereas PET nonresponders showed higher expression of matrix remodeling, neutrophil, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and angiogenesis genes, indicating a more active immune microenvironment in responders (Supplementary Fig. S5A).

Further analysis of the relationship between baseline GEP and pathologic response showed that type I IFN was the top signature enriched in tandem with pCR in PET responders. Baseline type I IFN signature correlated with pCR (P = 0.003) and MPR (P = 0.018) in PET responders (Supplementary Fig. S5B and S5C). In PET nonresponders, NOTCH pathway activation gene expression was the top signature enriched, with the signature score being higher in those without pCR (P = 0.039) or MPR (P = 0.023; Supplementary Fig. S5D and S5E).

Posttreatment analysis focused on non-pCR samples due to limited pCR/MPR tissue availability and revealed a potential reason for poor pathologic responses in patients who did not achieve pCR with their respective neoadjuvant treatments. In PET responders (n = 9), a heatmap analysis comparing the immune-related and tumor-intrinsic signature scores between baseline and posttreatment (Fig. 3A) showed an increase in CD8+ T cells (P = 0.077; Fig. 3B) and an upregulated checkpoint molecule signature score after treatment (P = 0.040; Fig. 3C). This indicated that the increased CD8+ T cells observed after treatment were likely in an exhausted state, characterized by impaired effector function despite tumor recognition due to inhibitory checkpoint expression. For PET nonresponders (n = 10), a heatmap analysis similar to that for PET responders (Fig. 3D) showed an upregulation in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) II signature score (P = 0.002; Fig. 3E) but lacked upregulation of effector cells (Supplementary Fig. S6A) and effector cell traffic signatures (Supplementary Fig. S6B) after treatment. This may be caused by the upregulation of immunosuppressive-related signatures such as immunosuppressive myeloid cells (Fig. 3F), tumor-associated macrophages (Supplementary Fig. S6C), and cancer-associated fibroblasts (Supplementary Fig. S6D).

Each row represents a gene signature, and the color scale ranges from blue (−0.15, decreased expression) to red (0.15, increased expression), representing the difference from baseline. sec.p: Lastly, PD-L1 TAP scores showed no significant difference between baseline and posttreatment in PET responders but increased significantly in nonresponders (P = 0.011; Supplementary Fig. S6E and S6F).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The RATIONALE-213 study indicates preliminary evidence about the efficacy and safety of tislelizumab in combination with chemotherapy or CRT as neoadjuvant treatment for resectable ESCC, utilizing the PET/CT-guided approach previously shown to be a good predictor of treatment response in esophageal cancer. The primary endpoint of the pCR rate showed promising results in both PET responders and nonresponders (30% and 34.4%, respectively). A sensitivity analysis counting nonsurgical patients as non-pCR yielded adjusted rates of 20% and 27.5%, respectively. The higher pCR rate in the PET nonresponders suggests that CRT may have a stronger local therapeutic effect. Both cohorts demonstrated favorable outcomes across secondary and exploratory endpoints, including 1-year DFS rates, 1-year EFS rates, ORR, 1-year OS rates, and MPR rates.

The pCR rate of 30% observed in PET responders treated with neoadjuvant tislelizumab plus chemotherapy in our study kept a relatively comparable performance with the 31.8% pCR rate reported by Greally and colleagues (14) in PET responders receiving traditional nCRT. These findings suggest that a neoadjuvant regimen containing tislelizumab and chemotherapy would be a valuable option for patients showing a good response to induction chemotherapy on PET assessment. Although this strategy could potentially reduce radiotherapy toxicities in selected patients, it requires further validation in randomized controlled trials. Recent studies in locally advanced ESCC highlight the evolving landscape of neoadjuvant strategies and the need for further investigation. Notably, the recent JCOG1109 NExT trial (26) demonstrated that triplet chemotherapy outperformed CRT in locally advanced ESCC and that CRT did not yield better outcomes than doublet chemotherapy.

The pCR rate was 34.4% in PET nonresponders in our study, whereas Greally and colleagues (14) reported a pCR rate of 11.1% in their study of PET nonresponders with ESCC treated with traditional nCRT. After a median follow-up of 25.5 months in our study, the median OS was NR for PET nonresponders, whereas in the study by Greally and colleagues (14), the reported median OS was 17.2 months. In the RATIONALE-213 study, PET nonresponders showed 1-year DFS and EFS rates of 74.2% and 67.8%, respectively. These results suggest potential benefits for PET nonresponders with PET/CT-guided neoadjuvant treatment with tislelizumab plus CRT. Considering the inherent differences in study design, treatment protocols, and patient populations between historical studies and RATIONALE-213, the potential survival benefit shown in this study still needs direct comparison through further phase III studies.

Our survival data, while immature, provide important context for the pCR findings. The encouraging 1-year EFS and OS rates in both PET responders and nonresponders should be interpreted cautiously, given the single-arm design and limited follow-up duration. The relatively higher survival rates in the PET responder cohort align with the established prognostic value of PET response (13–17). Notably, the median values for both EFS and OS were NR in either cohort, highlighting the need for longer follow-up to fully characterize the durability of benefit.

Several phase II studies investigating neoadjuvant immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy (without radiotherapy) in locally advanced ESCC have reported pCR rates ranging from 20% to 46.2% (27–31). The pCR rate in PET responders from the present study falls within this range. However, it is important to note that these phase II studies had small sample sizes (ranging from 13 to 51 patients), which may contribute to the considerable variation in reported pCR rates.

These findings contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting immunotherapy-based neoadjuvant approaches in ESCC, such as the Keystone-001 trial. Keystone-001 is a phase II trial that evaluated the efficacy and safety of preoperative treatment with pembrolizumab plus paclitaxel and cisplatin followed by Da Vinci robotic–assisted radical surgery in patients with locally advanced (stage III) ESCC. After a median follow-up of 23.3 months, the Keystone-001 trial reported a pCR rate of 42.2%, an ORR of 95.6%, a 1-year OS rate of 95.6%, and an MPR rate of 73.3%, with no grade ≥3 adverse events (32).

The high percentage of patients who completed neoadjuvant treatment in both cohorts (90% in PET responders and 85% in PET nonresponders) indicated good treatment compliance and tolerability of neoadjuvant tislelizumab treatment in combination with either chemotherapy or nCRT in the overall population. The high rates of R0 resection achieved in both cohorts (95% in PET responders and 90.6% in PET nonresponders) in RATIONALE-213 suggest that the PET-guided neoadjuvant treatment regimen with tislelizumab did not negatively affect surgical resectability in patients with ESCC, regardless of their initial PET response.

The proportion of patients who did not proceed to surgery—33.3% in the PET responder cohort and 20% in the PET nonresponder cohort—was higher than typically reported in similar studies (17% in NEOCRTEC5010 and 5.6% in CROSS). Patient refusal was the predominant reason across all studies. The small numbers preclude meaningful EFS/OS comparisons between surgical and nonsurgical groups. This limitation warrants investigation in future trials.

Preoperative best overall response showed potential predictive value for surgical outcomes in both cohorts. Patients achieving CRs or PRs were more likely to have favorable pathologic outcomes, including pCR or low residual tumor burden.

In exploratory analyses, patients with higher baseline tumor PD-L1 TAP scores in both cohorts showed higher pCR rates compared with those with lower PD-L1 TAP scores. Although these preliminary findings suggest that PD-L1 expression may be investigated as a potential biomarker for response to neoadjuvant tislelizumab-based therapy in ESCC, they require validation in larger studies.

The safety profile of tislelizumab combined with neoadjuvant chemotherapy or CRT was tolerable and consistent with known toxicities of the individual treatments. The radiotherapy dose used in this study (40 Gy) aligns with Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology guidelines (33) and recent landmark trials such as CROSS (41.4 Gy) and NEOCRTEC5010 (40 Gy), which demonstrated high pCR and R0 resection rates with reduced doses compared with standard clinical practice (5, 6). This approach was chosen to minimize treatment-related toxicity while maintaining efficacy, particularly considering the addition of immunotherapy, which might potentially enhance radiation side effects.

Exploratory biomarker analysis revealed a positive association of the type I IFN signature in PET responders achieving pCR and MPR and a negative association of NOTCH pathway activation with efficacy in PET nonresponders. These findings align with the RATIONALE-302 study biomarker results, which showed that type I IFN expression signatures were positively associated with the OS benefit of tislelizumab monotherapy and that NOTCH1 mutation leading to NOTCH pathway deficiency may potentially be a predictive biomarker for longer OS with tislelizumab versus chemotherapy (18.4 months vs. 5.3 months; HR, 0.35) in patients with advanced or metastatic ESCC (34). This suggests that these two pathways may play a specific role in immune response regulation in ESCC though our study assessed NOTCH pathway activation through RNA expression only, without DNA-based mutation analysis. RATIONALE-302 biomarker analysis showed NOTCH1 mutations correlated with both tislelizumab benefit and RNA expression changes similar to our findings, with mouse models confirming that NOTCH1 knockdown produced comparable immune effects (34).

In PET responders, neoadjuvant tislelizumab plus chemotherapy recruited more CD8+ T cells, but these T cells appeared exhausted, as indicated by upregulated checkpoint molecules (P = 0.014) in patients without a pCR. In PET nonresponders, neoadjuvant tislelizumab plus CRT significantly induced MHC II expression (P = 0.005), but the effector cells and the cytokines/chemokines necessary to recruit them were insufficiently represented in patients without a pCR, possibly owing to an increase in immunosuppressive immune and stromal cells. These findings indicate that PET nonresponders without pCR may develop an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment after treatment, potentially explaining their poor pathologic response to therapy. Other studies in ESCC using similar neoadjuvant immunotherapy and chemotherapy combinations have also reported the development of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy nonresponders (35, 36). Tumor-associated macrophages can inhibit T-cell function through various mechanisms, including the production of immunosuppressive cytokines and the expression of checkpoint molecules (37). Cancer-associated fibroblasts have been shown to contribute to this immunosuppressive environment by restricting CD8+ T-cell infiltration and promoting regulatory T-cell activity (36). Other immunosuppressive myeloid cells, such as myeloid-derived suppressor cells, can suppress T-cell responses and promote tumor progression through multiple pathways, including the production of reactive oxygen species and the depletion of essential amino acids required for T-cell function (38).

This study has several limitations. As a single-arm phase II trial without a randomized control arm, our study cannot definitively attribute the observed efficacy to the individual treatment components. This study was exploratory in nature, and all analyses were descriptive without formal hypothesis testing. Although the observed pCR rates are encouraging, their clinical relevance should be interpreted cautiously in the absence of mature OS and DFS data. The sample size in this study was relatively small, and the follow-up period was limited, necessitating longer-term data to confirm the durability of responses and impact on OS. Posttreatment samples from patients with pCR were not collected. Hence, the comparison of posttreatment changes between patients with a good pathologic response to neoadjuvant tislelizumab plus chemotherapy or tislelizumab plus CRT and patients with a poor response cannot be made. The biomarker analysis was limited to RNA sequencing without DNA-based mutation analysis. Due to the limited sample size, the biomarker findings from the retrospective analysis should be considered hypothesis-generating and require validation in additional datasets. As this was a phase II study, imaging and pathology assessments were performed locally without central review, and treatment heterogeneity in the PET nonresponder cohort could not be fully analyzed due to limited collection of center-level and radiotherapy planning data.

In conclusion, both PET-assessed responders and nonresponders in this phase II study who were treated with tislelizumab in combination with chemotherapy or CRT as neoadjuvant treatment for resectable ESCC achieved promising pCR rates and a tolerable safety profile. These preliminary findings warrant further investigation in randomized controlled trials to confirm the efficacy of this approach compared with standard treatment options.
